In his recent guest post on Noahpinion,
[Where's the "intelligence explosion"?](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/wheres-the-intelligence-explosion)
futurologist Ramez Naam explains why he's skeptical about Recursive Self-Improvement takeoff sometimes called
"FOOM"[^foom].

[^foom]: FOOM is not an acronym. It's the sound of a LOUD explosion.
    [Yudkowsky attributes it to IJ Good](https://youtube.com/watch?v=722LXkh5OGs&t=225s), but I couldn't find a
    clear citation.

The post is worth reading in its entirety, but in a nutshell there are many factors that could drive recursive
self-improvement. And the frontier labs are spending an absolute fortune applying AI to accelerating the development of
AI. Anthropic claim that
[26% of their AI research is led by AI](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development). It's also
why they are profitable
[unless you take into account the stupendous sums of money spent on developing the next AI](https://futurism.com/future-society/anthropic-claude-profit-ai-safety-development-finances).

Naam's point, buttressed by evidence from the labs themselves, is that these all face "diminishing returns".

![Key infographic from the Naam post, which acknowledges that AI is speeding up AI development, but claims this somehow falls short of "fast takeoff"](/assets/images/rsi-chart.webp){#fig-naam}

## The Maths Bit

Wisely, perhaps, he doesn't include a formula.

The underlying assumption is that the speed of **progress** (scientific, economic, etc.[^social]) is linked to the
current level of progress. The more progress we make, the faster progress becomes. Because, roughly, we're building and
improving tools all the time.

[^social]: We don't talk about social progress. The idea of social progress has the unmistakable whiff of socialism.
Indeed one might say the very idea of social progress is characteristic of socialism.

A simple mathematical model of this sort is that the speed with which progress, ahem, progresses (written
$\frac{dP}{dt}$) is proportional to the $k$-th power of the current level of progress ($P^k$).

$$
\frac{dP}{dt} \propto P^k
$$

This is a "differential equation" that characterizes the behaviour of the system. Solving it gives very different curves
depending on $k$: power-law growth for $k<1$, exponential growth for $k=1$, and a blow-up to infinity in finite time for
$k>1$.

What this means is that the behaviour of the system depends on the value we estimate for $k$.

We can fit it to data.

Naam cites the following evidence:

- At OpenAI, researchers used 124× more tokens per person and shipped about 7× as many lines of code, but ran only 1.6×
  as many experiments.
- At Anthropic, staff report a productivity uplift of around 4×. Naam reckons doubling the pace of progress would need
  about 40×.

From this he estimates that each extra point of AI capability (on Epoch's ECI benchmark) buys 2–3% more research
productivity, against the 15–19% needed for the loop to sustain itself. Very roughly, that puts $k$ at about 0.15. These
are the "diminishing returns".

Nothing to worry about, see?

## Straw Man Singularity ($K>1$)

Well no.

First up, it's worth noting that $k>1$ is utterly implausible. It hits infinity in finite time, which is not something
that anything actually does.

(move to footnote? needs to be accessible for general reader)

Suppose for the sake of argument that we're at progress level 0.1, and that $k=2$. We can show that the progress at time
$t$ is

$$
P(t) = \frac{0.1}{1 - 0.1t}
$$

So at time 10, the denominator goes to zero; progress has gone infinite.

Like the [Navier-Stokes result](FIXME) it points to a problem in our model. And it's not clear that anyone really
believes that $k>1$.

(Something about exponential) (Does anyone seriously claim k>1?)

Naam does seem to equate FOOM with k>1. That has to be a straw man.

## Subjective Singularity ($K\leq1$)

In general, futurologists do seem to believe that $k\leq1$. Kurzweil -- possibly the most influential thinker (did he
originate?) -- has spent a career arguing that $k=1$.

When $k=1$ the rate just keeps getting faster, forever. Progress never hits infinity, nor does the rate of progress. But
wait long enough and they are arbitrarily large. (Insert quote about how crazy this will feel -- centuries of innovation
in a week etc.)

And -- here's the thing -- $k<1$ is not much less bonkers. The "diminishing returns" are not a slowing to a halt. The
rate of progress keeps climbing forever, just ever more gently.

For all values of $k$ progress continues apace! When $k<1$ it still grows -- it never stops! -- but the rate of growth
decreases over time.

Either way, it's still a very strange world for primates who spent millennia figuring out how to use twigs to catch
ants.

But it doesn't have to be. $dP / dt$ is still ticking up and arguably it just has to be fast enough to give us future
shock. We don't need to stay exponential.

If say we start making mathematical breakthroughs every day, that's going to feel disorientating. It doesn't have to be
every hour.

Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei, for one, doesn't need an explosion to predict
[a "compressed 21st century"](https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/machines-of-loving-grace):

> AI-enabled biology and medicine will allow us to compress the progress that human biologists would have achieved over
> the next 50-100 years into 5-10 years.

And beyond a certain point, progress might be effectively infinite for our dumb primate brains.

Some weeks it feels like we're there already.

Alvin Toffler had a name for this back in 1970. "Future shock" is

> the shattering stress and disorientation that we induce in individuals by subjecting them to too much change in too
> short a time.
